title: Degrees of Freedom and Law of Equipartition of Energy
short_intro: Degrees of freedom represent the independent ways in which a dynamical system can store energy, corresponding to the coordinates necessary to specify its configuration. The law of equipartition of energy states that in thermal equilibrium, the total energy of a system is shared equally among all active degrees of freedom, with each degree contributing 1/2 k_B T per molecule.

exam_scope.tgt_core: Calculation of degrees of freedom for monoatomic, diatomic, and triatomic gas molecules; derivation of specific heat ratios (C_p / C_v); basic applications of the law of equipartition of energy.
exam_scope.pgt_extension: Advanced treatment of vibrational and rotational degrees of freedom at high temperatures, degrees of freedom of solids (Dulong-Petit law), and temperature-dependent behavior of specific heats of gases.

concept_notes.heading: Definition and Translational Degrees of Freedom
bullets: Degrees of freedom (f) are defined as the independent coordinates required to specify the position and configuration of a mechanical system.
Any free gas molecule moving in three-dimensional space possesses 3 translational degrees of freedom corresponding to motion along the X, Y, and Z axes.
Translational kinetic energy is given by 1/2 m v_x^2 + 1/2 m v_y^2 + 1/2 m v_z^2, yielding 1/2 k_B T per degree of freedom.

concept_notes.heading: Rotational and Vibrational Degrees of Freedom
bullets: Rotational degrees of freedom arise from rigid rotation about orthogonal axes passing through the center of mass.
Monoatomic gases have negligible moment of inertia about the atomic center, hence 0 rotational degrees of freedom.
Diatomic molecules have 2 rotational degrees of freedom at room temperature, while non-linear polyatomic molecules possess 3 rotational degrees of freedom.

concept_notes.heading: Law of Equipartition of Energy
bullets: Formulated by Boltzmann, this law states that for any dynamical system in thermal equilibrium, the total energy is equally distributed among all active degrees of freedom.
Each translational and rotational degree of freedom contributes an average energy of 1/2 k_B T per molecule (or 1/2 R T per mole).
Each vibrational degree of freedom contributes two terms (kinetic and potential), resulting in an average energy of k_B T per molecule (or R T per mole).

concept_notes.heading: Molar Heat Capacities and Adiabatic Exponent
bullets: Internal energy U of 1 mole of an ideal gas with f degrees of freedom is expressed as U = (f / 2) R T.
Molar heat capacity at constant volume C_v is defined as dU/dT = (f / 2) R.
Molar heat capacity at constant pressure C_p is given by C_v + R = (f / 2 + 1) R, leading to the ratio gamma = C_p / C_v = 1 + 2/f.

derivations.title: Derivation of Specific Heat Ratio (gamma) from Degrees of Freedom
derivations.conditions: Ideal gas with f degrees of freedom in thermal equilibrium
steps: Write the internal energy for one mole of an ideal gas: U = \frac{f}{2} R T.
Differentiate internal energy with respect to temperature to find molar heat capacity at constant volume: C_v = \frac{dU}{dT} = \frac{f}{2} R.
Apply Mayer's relation for ideal gases to find molar heat capacity at constant pressure: C_p = C_v + R = left(\frac{f}{2} + 1\right) R.
Take the ratio of C_p to C_v to obtain the adiabatic exponent: gamma = \frac{C_p}{C_v} = \frac{f/2 + 1}{f/2} = 1 + \frac{2}{f}.

derivations.title: Total Internal Energy of a Gas Mixture
derivations.conditions: Non-reacting mixture of ideal gases containing n_1, n_2 moles with degrees of freedom f_1, f_2
steps: Express the internal energy of the individual components as U_1 = \frac{f_1}{2} n_1 R T and U_2 = \frac{f_2}{2} n_2 R T.
Sum the internal energies to find the total internal energy of the mixture: U_{total} = U_1 + U_2 = left(\frac{f_1 n_1 + f_2 n_2}{2}\right) R T.
Define the effective degrees of freedom f_{mix} for the mixture using U_{total} = \frac{f_{mix}}{2} (n_1 + n_2) R T.
Equate and solve for f_{mix} to obtain the weighted average of degrees of freedom.

graphs_and_experiments.title: Temperature Dependence of Molar Heat Capacity (C_v) for Diatomic Gas
graphs_and_experiments.what_to_draw: A graph of C_v / R versus absolute temperature T, showing three distinct plateaus at 1.5R (low T, translational only), 2.5R (room T, translational + rotational), and 3.5R (high T, translational + rotational + vibrational).
graphs_and_experiments.interpretation: Degrees of freedom are activated sequentially as thermal energy increases, overcoming rotational and vibrational energy level spacings.
graphs_and_experiments.exam_use: Tested in conceptual multiple-choice questions regarding C_v values of diatomic gases at cryogenic versus high temperatures.

graphs_and_experiments.title: Maxwell-Boltzmann Energy Distribution
graphs_and_experiments.what_to_draw: Asymmetric bell-shaped curve plotting fraction of molecules versus molecular energy, illustrating the continuous spread of energy among molecules.
graphs_and_experiments.interpretation: While individual molecular energies fluctuate widely, the average energy per degree of freedom remains strictly fixed at 1/2 k_B T at a given temperature.
graphs_and_experiments.exam_use: Used to link statistical mechanics principles with macroscopic equipartition theorems.

graphs_and_experiments.title: Adiabatic versus Isothermal P-V Curves
graphs_and_experiments.what_to_draw: P-V diagram comparing isothermal (PV = constant) and adiabatic (PV^gamma = constant) curves originating from the same point, where the adiabatic curve is steeper due to gamma > 1.
graphs_and_experiments.interpretation: The steepness of the adiabatic curve directly reflects the value of gamma, which is determined by the degrees of freedom of the gas.
graphs_and_experiments.exam_use: Problem-solving involving work done during adiabatic expansions of monoatomic versus diatomic gases.

solved_numericals.question: Find the degrees of freedom and the ratio of specific heats (gamma) for a diatomic gas molecule at room temperature.
solution_steps: Identify the molecular structure: A diatomic gas molecule at room temperature has 3 translational and 2 rotational degrees of freedom.
Calculate total degrees of freedom: f = 3 + 2 = 5.
Use the formula for the ratio of specific heats: gamma = 1 + \frac{2}{f}.

solved_numericals.question: A mixture of 2 moles of helium (monoatomic, f = 3) and 3 moles of hydrogen (diatomic, f = 5, neglecting vibration) is contained in a vessel. Calculate the equivalent degrees of freedom and the ratio gamma for the mixture.
solution_steps: Identify parameters for gas 1 (Helium): n_1 = 2, f_1 = 3.
Identify parameters for gas 2 (Hydrogen): n_2 = 3, f_2 = 5.
Calculate effective degrees of freedom using f_{mix} = \frac{n_1 f_1 + n_2 f_2}{n_1 + n_2}.

solved_numericals.question: Calculate the molar heat capacity at constant volume (C_v) and constant pressure (C_p) for a non-linear triatomic gas molecule at high temperature where its vibrational mode is fully active. Take R = 8.314 J mol^{-1} K^{-1}.
solution_steps: Determine degrees of freedom for a non-linear triatomic molecule: 3 translational, 3 rotational, and let the number of vibrational modes be s = 3N - 6 = 3(3) - 6 = 3 vibrational modes.
Each vibrational mode contributes 2 degrees of freedom (kinetic and potential). Total degrees of freedom f = 3 (trans) + 3 (rot) + 2 \times 3 (vib) = 12.
Calculate C_v: C_v = \frac{f}{2} R = \frac{12}{2} R = 6 R.
Calculate C_p: C_p = C_v + R = 6R + R = 7R.
Substitute numerical value of R: C_v = 6 \times 8.314 = 49.88 J mol^{-1} K^{-1} and C_p = 7 \times 8.314 = 58.20 J mol^{-1} K^{-1}.

assumptions_and_limitations: The equipartition theorem assumes classical statistical mechanics, which breaks down at very low temperatures (cryogenic range) where quantum mechanical freezing of rotational and vibrational modes occurs.
Intermolecular forces are assumed to be negligible (ideal gas approximation), which fails at high pressures and low temperatures.

common_misconceptions.wrong: All degrees of freedom contribute equally to energy regardless of temperature.
common_misconceptions.correct: Degrees of freedom are temperature-dependent and freeze out at lower temperatures.
common_misconceptions.why: Quantum mechanical energy level spacings exceed thermal energy kT at low temperatures, making certain modes inactive.

common_misconceptions.wrong: Monoatomic gases possess rotational degrees of freedom.
common_misconceptions.correct: Monoatomic gases have zero rotational degrees of freedom.
common_misconceptions.why: Rotation of a point mass or sphere about its center of mass produces no change in spatial configuration or moment of inertia.

common_misconceptions.wrong: Vibrational energy contributes 1/2 k_B T per mode to internal energy.
common_misconceptions.correct: Vibrational energy contributes k_B T per mode.
common_misconceptions.why: Vibration possesses both kinetic and potential energy terms, each contributing 1/2 k_B T according to the equipartition theorem.
